summary: Offers advice to people designing link layers and local networks that must carry Internet protocols. It explains how design choices such as packet size, error handling and delay affect how well IP and TCP work, drawing on lessons from past designs. It is a Best Current Practice.

eli5.summary: If you build a new kind of road, this guide tells you what shape and rules will let all the usual delivery trucks use it without trouble.

questions: how link design affects tcp performance
what mtu should a new link use
subtitle: What link-layer and local-network designers should know so their technology works well with IP and TCP.

tldr.problem: Designers of link layers and local networks often know little about the Internet architecture, and choices they make about packet size, error recovery or delay can quietly hurt IP and TCP performance.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC walks through the design areas that matter (MTU, framing, broadcast and multicast, error control, delay, buffering, compression, reordering, mobility, routing and security) and says what IP and TCP expect from each.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice (BCP 89) that stresses keeping subnetwork features lightweight and leaving reliability and security to the end points. It has since been updated by RFC 9599.

facts.label: Minimum error detection
facts.value: At least as strong as a 32-bit CRC

today: RFC 3819 is a Best Current Practice that has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 9599, so read the two together. The text itself dates from July 2004 and speaks of ECN and IPv6 as newer or less widely deployed.

sections.title: Who the Advice Is For
sections.content:
The RFC is written for designers of digital communication equipment, link-layer protocols and packet-switched local networks, together called subnetworks, who want to carry Internet protocols. A subnetwork here is a layer 2 network that sits immediately below IP and does not rely on IP routers to forward packets inside it.

Optimizing a subnetwork for IP involves three things: providing enough functionality to carry IP, removing unnecessary functions that add cost or complexity, and choosing parameters that maximize the performance of Internet protocols. Because IP is so simple, the authors say designers make many more errors of commission than of omission.

A recurring theme is the end-to-end principle. Functions such as reliable delivery and cryptography can be implemented properly only at the end points, so duplicating them inside the subnetwork can be redundant or even harmful. Partial duplication is sometimes justified, for example link-layer retransmission on a lossy mobile radio channel, but only with an understanding of how it interacts with higher layers.
sections.eli5: A road builder should know how delivery trucks work. Mostly the road should just carry them, and the trucks themselves make sure the parcels arrive.

sections.title: Packet Size and Framing
sections.content:
IPv4 packets range from 20 bytes (the header alone) to 65535 bytes. A subnetwork's largest packet is its Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU). The Internet community has concluded that router fragmentation is best avoided, so subnetworks should support "reasonably" large MTUs. All IPv4 hosts must accept 576-byte packets, which would be inefficient, and IPv6 sets a minimum MTU of 1280 bytes. A subnetwork with a smaller internal payload must fragment and reassemble internally if it is to support IPv6. Ethernet's 1500 bytes limits the usefulness of larger MTUs elsewhere, yet larger ones are still encouraged on high-speed links. Tunneling adds header overhead and has increased the incidence of path MTU black holes.

On slow links the opposite pressure applies. Interactive response should stay within the human-factors limit of 100 to 200 ms. A 1500-byte packet takes about 8 ms on a T1 link (1.536 Mb/s) but 625 ms at 19.2 kb/s, and a 256-byte MTU brings that to a little over 100 ms. The RFC calls this a fundamental trade-off between efficiency and latency, and notes that too small an MTU raises header overhead.

IP also needs the subnetwork to mark where each variable-length packet begins and ends. Where the subnetwork uses fixed-size units (ATM cells carry a 48-octet payload plus a 5-octet header), an adaptation layer is needed. The RFC describes three approaches: pad the last unit and mark first/last (as AAL5 does), carry a pointer to the end of the packet (as MPEG-2 Transport Streams do), or insert flag sequences between packets (as PPP's HDLC-based framing does).
sections.eli5: Big boxes carry more per trip but take a long time to load on a slow conveyor belt. Small boxes get through fast but waste more on packing. A designer has to pick a size that suits the belt.

sections.title: Connections, Broadcast and Multicast
sections.content:
IP is connectionless. Connection-oriented subnetworks such as ATM can carry it, but usually with a shim layer, the Subnetwork Dependent Convergence Function, that opens connections when a packet is queued and closes them after an idle timeout. Traffic is bursty, so the timeout is hard to choose: too short stresses connection management, too long wastes resources. Purely connectionless subnets such as Ethernet are the best match for best-effort IP. Bandwidth on Demand (BoD) subnets grant transmission opportunities on request; they should be able to extend a hold on the channel for data that arrives after the request, and they can cause spurious TCP timeouts when the data rate drops.

Many IPv4 protocols rely on broadcast: ARP, RARP, BOOTP, DHCP and RIP. Without it, some may be hampered or fail outright (DHCP is the example given), so shared links should support native link-layer broadcast. IPv6 uses multicast instead.

Multicast is much more efficient when the subnetwork supports it natively. Shared-channel subnetworks should reserve part of their own address space for multicast, and interfaces should accept several dozen multicast addresses. Switched subnetworks must at least reach all group members, by flooding or by using group membership information from IGMP or MLD.
sections.eli5: Shouting to the whole room is how some protocols find each other, so a new network needs a way to shout. If it can also whisper to just one group at a time, everyone saves effort.

sections.title: Reliability and Error Control
sections.content:
Ultimate responsibility for error recovery lies at the end points, so subnetwork reliability should be "lightweight": good enough, not perfect. Two tools are named. ARQ (Automatic Repeat Request) detects errors and requests retransmission. Forward Error Correction (FEC) adds enough redundancy to correct some errors without retransmitting, and is normally part of the physical layer.

Link-layer and TCP retransmission can compete. When the link layer retransmits, latency rises, which may trigger an unnecessary TCP retransmission of a packet the link is still resending. The RFC defines link-layer ARQ persistency as the maximum time a link spends trying to deliver a packet. If the link cannot tell flows apart (for example because of network layer encryption), persistency should be small. If it can, persistency should be high for flows using reliable transports such as TCP and low for all other flows, with a practical upper limit of 30 to 60 seconds.

For outages, the RFC says there is no standard way to tell TCP that the subnetwork is down rather than congested, so TCP backs off exponentially. A subnetwork should not silently discard packets during an outage; holding even a few packets per connection lets delivery tell TCP the link is back.

On error detection, any new subnetwork designed to carry IP should provide detection for each IP packet at least as strong as the 32-bit CRC in ISO 3309. End-to-end checksums remain essential, because corruption also comes from bugs in hosts and routers. Applications that tolerate corrupt payloads, such as voice codecs, can use UDP-Lite.
sections.eli5: If the postman and the receiver both keep resending the same letter, the mailbox fills with copies. The road should try a little to deliver, but the sender and receiver are the ones who make sure it truly arrives.

sections.title: TCP Performance and Delay
sections.content:
The RFC explains how TCP works so link designers can predict its behavior. TCP treats packet loss as a sign of congestion, shrinks its congestion window, and then grows it again (slow start, then additive increase and multiplicative decrease). Three duplicate acknowledgments trigger a fast retransmit, and Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN), which was a proposed standard and not yet widely deployed at the time, lets routers signal congestion without dropping packets. Because ECN stays optional, a missing ECN bit must never be read as a lack of congestion.

For throughput, it gives two formulae. The simple upper bound is BW = C * MSS / (RTT * sqrt(p)) with C equal to 0.93; the fuller Reno formula also accounts for retransmission timeouts. In the worked example, a wireless link that loses 1% of packets with a 20 ms one-way delay, on a path with a 120 ms round trip and a 1000-byte MSS, yields about 666 kbit/s from the simple formula and 402.9 kbit/s from the complex one. That is disappointing on a 2 Mb/s link. The RFC also warns that real bit errors are not independent, so a loss rate computed from the bit-error ratio is only an upper bound.

Other lessons: TCP's timeout algorithm copes poorly when delay variance and loss are both high, so designers should minimize delay, delay variance and loss; ARQ raises delay variance while FEC does not. Heavy bandwidth asymmetry slows the return of ACKs and hurts TCP. For buffering, a rule of thumb is one link bandwidth times delay product per TCP connection, and active queue management such as RED is widely considered better than tail drop. ATM subnets should discard the remaining fragments of an IP packet once one is lost.
sections.eli5: A delivery truck slows down every time a parcel goes missing, and it cannot tell why. So a road that loses parcels, even by accident, makes every truck crawl.

sections.title: QoS, Compression, Reordering, Mobility and Routing
sections.content:
Quality of service. The RFC describes the two IETF approaches: Integrated Services (Intserv), with per-flow reservations, and Differentiated Services (Diffserv), which marks aggregates with a codepoint (DSCP) that selects a per-hop behavior. It lists capabilities a subnetwork might offer, such as bandwidth reservation based on a token bucket model, letting unused reserved bandwidth go to other flows, and telling IP how much fixed delay and jitter it offers.

Compression. Application data compression can usually be omitted from the subnetwork, since data may already be compressed or encrypted and a compressor must never expand it. The RFC strongly recommends that low-speed or small-MTU subnetworks compress IP and transport headers. An uncompressed 40-byte TCP/IP header takes about 33 ms at 9600 bps, while VJ header compression shrinks most to 3 to 5 bytes. Compressors depend on in-order delivery and can magnify the effect of losses.

Reordering. Three duplicate ACKs make TCP halve its congestion window, so heavy reordering hurts. Subnetworks should avoid reordering where possible, but not at the cost of efficiency, reliability or delay.

Mobility and routing. Subnetworks may offer internal mobility, as Ethernet switching and cellular handoff do, but large ones should use nearest-exit routing. IP assumes a multipoint subnetwork has uniform metrics between members and that it is stable on a routing timescale of tens of seconds. Subnetworks that span large areas or mix very different links should be avoided, or must provide compensating mechanisms, and designers should reuse existing routing protocols where they can.
sections.eli5: A good road builder also thinks about priority lanes, packing parcels smaller, keeping them in order, letting trucks change roads, and not inventing a new map system when a good one exists.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states a "security placement principle": a security mechanism is most effective close to, and under the control of, the owner of the asset it protects. Its corollary is that end-to-end security cannot be ensured by subnetwork mechanisms. The working group did not reach consensus on whether designers should be encouraged to protect user data, but it held a clear consensus that weak or incorrectly implemented subnetwork security may be counterproductive, because it can give a false sense of security. Designers who do add it should be candid about its limits.

There is clear consensus for subnetworks protecting themselves against theft of service and denial of service. The RFC also suggests that subnetworks authenticate the source of a frame, which would help with weaknesses in address resolution such as ARP, and it urges extreme care with mechanisms meant to defeat traffic analysis.

Past mistakes it lists include untested algorithms, security by obscurity, trapdoors, sending passwords in clear text, keys shared by every system on a subnet, poorly designed initialization vectors, and identifying information sent in clear text.
sections.eli5: A lock on one door does not make the whole house safe. The best locks are on the things you actually want to protect, and a flimsy lock can make people careless.

viz.caption: WHAT SUBNETWORK DESIGNERS SHOULD MINIMIZE FOR TCP

items.title: Delay
items.text: Excessive delay limits how well TCP can fill a fast pipe and slows loss recovery.

items.title: Delay variance
items.text: High variance forces a large retransmission timeout. ARQ increases it; FEC does not.

items.title: Packet loss
items.text: TCP reads loss as congestion, so link losses cut throughput.
